messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The event that reshaped Tran’s life happened forty-two years ago, but in his mind it has never ended. His daughter, Linh, was three years old when a sudden bacterial infection sent her into septic shock. For eleven days he sat beside her hospital bed, watching monitors flicker and listening to the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator. The antiseptic smell—that sharp, chemical overlay of bleach and alcohol—lodged itself so deeply in his memory that even now, decades later, catching that scent in a hallway or a doctor’s waiting room can drop him straight back into the fluorescent-lit room where his child’s skin had turned a waxy grey. He had been a systems analyst even then, a man who believed in protocols and predictable outcomes, and the utter helplessness of those hours hollowed him out in a way he never fully recovered from.

Linh survived, grew up, had children of her own. Tran retired from his cybersecurity firm at seventy, but boredom drove him back to part-time consulting. He still works from a small home office, monitoring network traffic for a financial services company. The work suits him: it is logical, contained, and nothing about it smells like a hospital. But the world outside his office door has become increasingly treacherous. When his daughter recently announced she was pregnant again, the news did not bring him joy. Instead, it triggered a cascade of visceral dread. The sight of her growing belly, the sound of her voice discussing baby names—these reminders of pregnancy and birth felt less like happy milestones and more like the opening of a door he had spent four decades trying to keep shut. His mind would instantly supply the image of Linh as a tiny, grey-faced child, and the memory would flood back with such force that he could feel the cold vinyl of the visitor’s chair beneath his hands, hear the ventilator’s rhythm, taste the metallic tang of fear at the back of his throat. The memory did not feel like a recollection; it felt like the present tense, a live feed he could not turn off. When he tried to explain this to his son-in-law, he found himself losing the thread, his sentences fragmenting into silence, because the words did not exist to bridge the gap between a healthy adult woman and the dying toddler he still saw in his mind’s eye.

These intrusions fed on themselves. The more the memories came—playing over like a film he could not pause—the more vigilant he became for anything that might trigger them again. A routine physical examination last month became an ordeal. The moment the doctor’s stethoscope touched his chest, the antiseptic smell hit him, and his heart began to pound so violently that the physician asked if he was in pain. Tran could not answer. He was not in the examination room anymore; he was back in the pediatric ICU, watching the respiratory therapist adjust Linh’s oxygen saturation monitor. The physical reactivity—the racing pulse, the shallow breathing, the tremor in his hands—only deepened his sense that the event was not over. He had come to believe that his own body was unreliable, that any strong emotion could hijack him and drop him into that past moment without warning. This fear of negative feelings, of the shame and horror that accompanied the flashbacks, made him avoid not only hospitals but any conversation that might drift toward illness, childhood, or family health. He stopped attending family gatherings where grandchildren might talk about school illnesses. He screened his daughter’s calls when he was not prepared to hear her voice, because her tone alone—even a cheerful one—could trigger the memory of her weak, fevered whisper.

The cycle tightened over the months. Each trigger—a baby on a bus, a discussion of vaccines at work, the faint bleach smell from a cleaning cart in his office building—activated the memory, and each reactivation made the memory feel more immediate, more inescapable. The film played more frequently. He began to feel as though he was losing his grip on time itself. The past was no longer past; it was a parallel channel running beneath his daily life, ready to surface at any moment. His concentration at work suffered. He missed a critical anomaly in a log file because his mind had drifted to the hospital corridor, and his supervisor—kindly but firmly—suggested he take a leave of absence. That conversation, too, became a trigger: the supervisor’s concerned tone sounded, to Tran’s ears, exactly like the doctor who had once said, “We’re doing everything we can.”

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of quiet terror. Last week, cleaning out a closet, he found an old baby blanket of Linh’s, folded and yellowed. The fabric held no smell—it had been washed a hundred times—but the sight of it was enough. He spent the next three hours on the floor of his bedroom, his back against the wall, unable to move, fully convinced that if he stood up, he would find himself in a hospital room in 1982, and this time his daughter would not survive. When the fog lifted, he called his doctor. He is afraid of what therapy might unearth, but he is more afraid of living inside a memory that refuses to become the past.
